23.0.0.en: This is an introduction that God gives about the feasts. He calls them seasons and also holy convocations, which are proclaimed to all the people by means of trumpets so that they may take notice and be occupied with the feast rather than their ordinary work, to remember the spiritual meaning that God intends by the feast.

23.1.1.en: Just as God rested from His works in the creation of the world on the seventh day, so He commanded in the Fourth Commandment to keep the Sabbath day holy, that is, to set it apart for the worship of God. Material work is not done on it, but prayers are lifted up and sacrifices are offered, and only the necessary material tasks are done, such as giving food and drink to their animals.

23.1.2.en: The Jews laid down many specific material rules for the Sabbath, to prevent work and to permit walking a set distance ... and they neglected the spiritual side. But Christ made clear that the purpose of the Sabbath is the worship and service of God and not merely stopping work (Mt 12:9-13). In the New Testament the glory of Sunday surpassed that of the Sabbath, because on it Christ rose from the dead; therefore the Lord's Day in the New Testament is Sunday, while the Sabbath day is also honored because on it God completed the creation of the world and rested, that is, was pleased with what He had made, so we please Him by worship and service.

23.1.3.en: Take care to distinguish the Lord's Day with more worship and service than the other days, remembering His love for you, for He rose to raise you from the preoccupations of the world and to let you enjoy fellowship with Him.

23.2.s.en: (2) The Feasts of the Passover and Unleavened Bread

23.2.0.en: After mentioning the Sabbath day, which the Ten Commandments enjoin, He proclaimed the great feasts of the Jews, which are seven:

23.3.0.en: The Feast of the Passover is a remembrance of what they did when they went out of the land of Egypt, where God rescued them from slavery and saved their firstborn from death. It was held on the fourteenth day of the first month, which is the month of Abib, called Nisan after the captivity. It is the first month of the religious year, which corresponds to the seventh month of the civil year, and corresponds today to the months of March and April. This feast was already mentioned and explained in (Ex 12:1-14), and is also mentioned in (Num 28) and (Deut 16:6). It was held between the two evenings, that is, between the ninth and the eleventh hour by Jewish reckoning, which is between three and five in the afternoon by present-day reckoning. It clearly signifies Christ the Redeemer (1 Cor 5:7), who died for us on the Cross.

23.4.0.en: The Feast of Unleavened Bread is the second feast of the Jews and follows the Passover directly, that is, on the fifteenth day of the first month, and is kept for seven days, in remembrance of the children of Israel taking their dough before it was leavened and going out quickly from Egypt. Its taste is not as good as leavened bread, so it signifies the misery that the children of Israel suffered in Egypt. Unleavened bread also signifies purity and sincerity, and Christ, who was distinguished by these qualities (1 Cor 5:8). In the Church of the New Testament, however, leavened bread is offered, because Christ offered leavened bread on Maundy Thursday. Leaven signifies evil, for Christ bore our sins on the Cross and died for us.

23.5.0.en: The Feast of Unleavened Bread is kept on the first day, that is, the fifteenth, and the seventh, that is, the twenty-first of the first month, and on them they free themselves for worship and leave their material work. During the days of the Feast of Unleavened Bread these sacrifices are offered every day (Num 28:17-25:)

23.5.1.en: 1- Burnt offerings, which are two young bullocks, one ram and seven lambs of the first year, in addition to three tenths of flour mingled with oil for each bullock, two tenths for the ram, and one tenth for each lamb.

23.5.2.en: 2- A sin offering, which is a kid of the goats.

23.5.3.en: 3- The daily burnt offering with its drink offerings in the morning and evening (Num 28:3-10).

23.5.5.en: Remember every morning Christ, who died for you so that you might live for Him, when you pray the prime hour and remember His holy Resurrection, so that your aim on this day is to respond to His love with worship and doing good.

23.6.0.en: The third feast is the Feast of Firstfruits, that is, offering the first sheaf of the harvest of their crops, which was of barley because it ripens before other crops such as wheat. Of course this feast began after the children of Israel entered the Promised Land and cultivated the land.

23.6.1.en: Offering the firstfruits of animals and crops has spiritual meanings, the most important of which are:

23.6.2.en: 1- Declaring that God is the giver of all good things, of animals and of plants, so we give Him from His own hand.

23.6.4.en: 3- God's blessing on the remainder that man uses.

23.6.5.en: 4- Supporting the priests and the Levites consecrated to the service of the temple.

23.6.6.en: And this feast falls within the Feasts of the Passover and Unleavened Bread.

23.7.0.en: Wave: he carries it on his hands and moves it in the four directions, that is, it is offered to God who fills every place.

23.7.1.en: The priest takes the sheaf and waves it before God in one of the following ways:

23.7.2.en: 1- He waves the sheaf as it is, with its ears, after dipping it in oil, then takes a handful of it and offers it on the altar with the frankincense, and the rest is eaten by him and the priests.

23.7.3.en: 2- The sheaf is beaten with a rod to separate the grains from the straw, then the grains are roasted on the fire and oil is put on them, and then the priest offers a handful of it on the altar with the frankincense, and the rest is eaten by the priests.

23.7.4.en: 3- The grains are ground and the flour is kneaded with oil, then the priest takes a handful of it and offers it with the frankincense on the altar, and the rest is eaten by the priests.

23.7.5.en: And the sheaf of firstfruits signifies Christ, the Firstborn among many brethren, who offered Himself on the Cross to the Father and redeemed us.

23.7.6.en: The sheaf is offered on the morrow after the Sabbath, and what is meant by the morrow after the Sabbath is:

23.7.7.en: 1- Either the Sunday following the Sabbath that falls during the days of the Feast of Unleavened Bread, as the Sadducees among the Jews hold.

23.7.8.en: 2- Counting the first day of Unleavened Bread, which is the fifteenth of the first month, as the day of rest on which no work is done and which is consecrated to God, so that it is the Sabbath, because the word sabbath means rest; consequently the Feast of Firstfruits is the sixteenth day of the first month, and this is the opinion of the Pharisees.

23.8.0.en: At the Feast of Firstfruits, in addition to the first sheaf of the harvest, the following are offered:

23.8.1.en: 1- A he lamb without blemish of the first year as a burnt offering.

23.8.2.en: 2- Two tenths of fine flour mingled with oil, which equals 6.4 liters, and wine is poured on it in the amount of a fourth part of a hin, that is, one liter.

23.8.3.en: The lamb signifies Christ the Redeemer, who pleased the Father by the sacrifice of Himself; the flour mingled with oil signifies the purity of the life of Christ in the flesh, in which is the oil, that is, the Holy Spirit; and the wine signifies the joy that Christ brought into our hearts by His redemption.

23.8.4.en: To the offerings of the Feast of Firstfruits are added the offerings that are offered in the days of Unleavened Bread, mentioned in the explanation of (vv. 7, 8).

23.9.0.en: Parched corn: green grains of wheat after being roasted or grilled.

23.9.1.en: Green ears: green ears of wheat.

23.9.2.en: The Law forbids eating of the grains of the new harvest, barley or wheat, in any form before the first sheaf is offered at the Feast of Firstfruits, and during the days of Unleavened Bread they eat from the old harvest, because it is God who takes first from the harvest, and so blesses the rest, and then the people eat of it.

23.9.3.en: The Feast of Firstfruits signifies the Resurrection of Christ, who rose as the firstfruits of those who have fallen asleep, and it comes on the third day of the Passover. And while the Jews were celebrating the Feast of Firstfruits in the year of the crucifixion of Christ, He rose from the dead on the same day, so the Feast of Firstfruits signifies His Resurrection.

23.9.4.en: Make sure that God has a share in all your good things, so you give Him the firstfruits of your money, your possessions, your crops and all that He gives you, and so receive His blessing in your life; and offer firstfruits of every kind to the needy, so that all rejoice with one heart because they are members of the one body of Christ, that is, the Church.

23.10.0.en: The morrow after the Sabbath: Sunday.

23.10.1.en: The day that ye brought the sheaf of the wave offering: that is, the day of the Feast of Firstfruits, which is the first of the days of the Feast of Unleavened Bread and which follows the Passover, as we mentioned.

23.10.3.en: The morrow after the seventh sabbath: corresponds to the fiftieth day from the Feast of Firstfruits.

23.10.4.en: The day of Pentecost comes fifty days after the Feast of Firstfruits and is a Sunday, just as the Feast of Firstfruits is a Sunday, and at the Feast of Pentecost special offerings are brought near to God.

23.10.5.en: The Feast of the Fiftieth Day is also called the Feast of Pentecost, whose meaning in the Greek language is fiftieth (Acts 2:1, 20:16); it is also called the Feast of Weeks because it comes seven weeks after the Feast of Firstfruits (Ex 34:22, Deut 16:10). It is also called the Feast of Harvest because on it the harvest of wheat and the rest of the winter crops is completed (Ex 23:16). They also call it the Feast of Firstfruits because on it the firstfruits of the wheat harvest are offered.

23.10.6.en: It is clear that the celebration of this feast began after the children of Israel entered the Promised Land and cultivated wheat and the other crops. The Feast of Pentecost is one of the most important feasts among the Jews, because on it all the men must come to the house of the Lord in Jerusalem, as also happens at the Feasts of the Passover and Tabernacles.

23.10.7.en: This feast comes in the third month of the religious year, which is called Sivan; it corresponds to the ninth month of the civil year and today corresponds to the months of May and June. The purpose of this feast is:

23.10.8.en: 1- To thank God for His gifts of the winter crops, the most important of which is wheat, and that He completed His work with His people and gave them His good things.

23.10.9.en: 2- A remembrance of God's giving the commandments to Moses on the mountain, since the Jews believed that the commandments were given fifty days after their departure from the land of Egypt.

23.10.10.en: Because of the importance of this feast, the Jews offered repentance and confession of their sins and washed on it as a symbol of their purity, in addition to spending the night of the feast in praising God.

23.10.11.en: At the end of (v. 16) it says "ye shall offer a new meat offering unto the LORD," and what is meant is offering the first sheaf of the wheat harvest, which is apart from the first offering, that is, the first sheaf of the barley harvest, which they offered at the Feast of Firstfruits.

23.10.12.en: The Feasts of the Passover and Unleavened Bread signify the toil and hardship that the children of Israel endured in slavery in Egypt, from which God brought them out by the plague on the firstborn, in which they slaughtered the Passover. The Feasts of Firstfruits and Pentecost signify joy at receiving God's blessings and good things. And if the Feast of the Passover signifies the death of Christ on the Cross and the Feast of Firstfruits signifies His Resurrection, then the Feast of Pentecost signifies the descent of the Holy Spirit, who in fact descended on the Church on it and founded it.

23.11.0.en: Your habitations: your fields in the land of Canaan.

23.11.2.en: Two tenth deals: each loaf is made of a tenth of an ephah, that is, 2.3 liters.

23.11.3.en: They used to make two large loaves, each about 70 cm by 40 cm in size and about 10 cm thick, baked with leavened flour because they represent their daily food, and they offer them to God to bless all their foods. No part of them is offered on the altar, because no leaven is placed on the altar, as it signifies evil (Lev 2:11); so they are only waved before God, that is, the priests carry them on their hands and move them in the four directions of the world, declaring God's blessing on all their fields and foods, and then the priests eat them as a symbol of God's acceptance of their offerings. The two loaves signify:

23.11.4.en: 1- God's blessing on their earthly life, that is, their material work, and also their heavenly life, that is, their worship of God.

23.11.5.en: 2- The two loaves signify the Jews and the Gentiles, for Christ came for the salvation of the whole world.

23.11.6.en: 3- The number (2) signifies love, that is, their love for God and for one another.

23.11.7.en: 4- The priests' eating of the two loaves signifies God's blessing in the sacrament of the priesthood, to give the priests strength to carry out their service.

23.12.0.en: The offerings that are offered at this feast are:

23.12.1.en: a- Basic offerings, which are those mentioned here in the Book of Leviticus, and include:

23.12.3.en: A young bullock with its offering, which is three tenths of flour mingled with oil, as mentioned in (Num 28:26-31).

23.12.4.en: Two rams with their offerings, which are two tenths of flour mingled with oil for each ram.

23.12.5.en: Seven lambs of the first year, that is, each one a year old, with their offerings, which are a tenth of an ephah of flour mingled, that is, kneaded with oil, for each lamb.

23.12.6.en: 2- A sin offering, which is a kid of the goats.

23.12.7.en: 3- A peace offering, which is two lambs of the first year.

23.12.8.en: b- Additional sacrifices, which are those mentioned in the Book of Numbers (Num 28:26-31), and include:

23.12.10.en: Two young bullocks with their offerings, which are three tenths of flour mingled with oil for each bullock.

23.12.11.en: A ram with its offering, which is two tenths of flour mingled with oil.

23.12.12.en: Seven lambs of the first year with their offerings, which are one tenth of flour mingled with oil for each lamb.

23.12.13.en: 2- A sin offering, which is a kid of the goats.

23.12.14.en: c- Voluntary sacrifices, that is, freewill offerings, which the people offer to God for the priests and the Levites to eat of, and which are mentioned in the Book of Deuteronomy (Deut 16:9-12).

23.12.15.en: d- The daily burnt offering in the morning and evening, which is mentioned in (Ex 29:38-42).

23.13.0.en: The two lambs: what is meant is the two lambs of the peace offering.

23.13.1.en: The priest waves part of the sin offerings and peace offerings, which are the right thigh and the breast, that is, he moves them in the four directions before God, and then the priest and his household take them, with the two loaves also, as already mentioned in (v. 17). "They shall be holy to the LORD for the priest": the priest eats of them, as already explained in the sin offering (ch. 6:

23.14.0.en: The priests blow the trumpets and call the people to celebrate this feast, and each one leaves his material work and gives himself wholly to worship on this day.

23.14.1.en: Keeping this feast is a necessary command that God enjoined on the children of Israel to do throughout their days, as long as there are priests of the seed of Aaron, until Christ comes, whom all these sacrifices signify.

23.14.2.en: The full celebration of this feast was after they entered the land of Canaan and reaped the wheat, but the children of Israel began to celebrate it in part, by offering the sacrifices mentioned without the two loaves, in the wilderness of Sinai, in remembrance of Moses' receiving the Law.

23.14.3.en: In the New Testament we remember the feast in the Feast of Pentecost, which is the "Feast of the Fiftieth Day," the remembrance of the descent of the Holy Spirit on the Church, and we also remember Moses' receiving the Law in the prayer of the prostration, and much incense is offered in a large censer in remembrance of the sight of Mount Sinai full of fire and smoke when the Law was received.

23.15.0.en: Here God stresses His concern for the poor, so He repeats His commandment that He mentioned in (ch. 19:9, 10) and then repeated in (Deut 24:19-22), concerning the harvest of the fields: they leave the corners of their fields with their ears of grain, or the gleanings of the harvest, that is, the grains scattered on the ground, for the poor to gather, so that they may find food for themselves.

23.15.1.en: Let the feast be an opportunity to take care to visit the poor, the needy, the sick and everyone who is going through a distress, such as the death of a relative, so that you offer them love and they rejoice with you in this feast.

23.16.0.en: On the first day of the seventh month of the religious year, which corresponds to the first month in the civil year, which is the month of Tishri or Tishrin the First, also called Ethanim (1 Kgs 8:2), and which corresponds today to the month of September or October, the priests blow trumpets made of the horn of a sheep, with a mouthpiece of gold, or silver trumpets. At the Feast of Atonement, however, the trumpets were made of the horn of a ram. The trumpets have forms that are attached with the explanation.

23.16.1.en: The priests used to blow trumpets at this feast from its eve until the morning, and the people could blow other trumpets in their own places; on the Sabbath, however, the priests blew inside the house of the Lord and not outside it. The trumpets of the priests. This feast is called the Feast of Trumpets or the Feast of Shouting because they blow trumpets on it and shout with loud voices, glorifying God.

23.16.2.en: Blowing the trumpets at this feast, besides the other feasts, was used to gather the people at the beginnings of months and the various religious convocations, and also when calling them to war or for any other purposes. The Feast of Trumpets has many spiritual meanings, among them:

23.16.3.en: 1- Thanking God for His kindnesses and mercies throughout the past year, for it is the close of the civil year and the gathering of the summer crops.

23.16.4.en: 2- The feast coincides with the beginning of a new civil year and the sowing of the seeds of the winter crops, that is, the beginning of the new cultivation, so they ask God's blessing and prepare for a new spiritual beginning with Him, and remind Him of His covenants with their fathers so that He may bless them, and they pledge to live with Him.

23.16.5.en: 3- The supreme council of the Jews (the Sanhedrin) decided that the Feast of Trumpets is a remembrance of the redemption of Isaac by a ram, that is, they remember God's redemption of them and His rescue of them from the slavery of Egypt, and all this signifies Christ the Redeemer in the fullness of time.

23.16.6.en: 4- A remembrance of the giving of the Law on the mountain when they heard the sound of the trumpets (Ex 19:14-19); it declares the importance of the word of God and living by it.

23.16.7.en: 5- This feast is a preparation for the following feasts in the same month, which are the Feast of Atonement and the Feast of Tabernacles, feasts of the greatest importance among the Jews, whose details will come shortly in this chapter.

23.16.8.en: 6- This feast reminds them of keeping the seventh day, which is the Sabbath, holy, and of keeping the seventh year holy, and then the year of Jubilee, which comes after seven weeks, because this feast comes at the beginning of the seventh month.

23.16.9.en: 7- In the Feast of Trumpets God calls His people to obtain salvation and confirms their hope in Him; it signifies their return from captivity and then faith in Christ (Isa 27:13), and it also signifies the Second Coming of Christ at the sound of the trumpets mentioned in the Book of Revelation (Rev 8-11).

23.17.0.en: Like the other feasts, the people free themselves for the worship of God and leave their material work.

23.17.1.en: The fire offering brought near to the Lord at the feast was:

23.17.2.en: a- The morning burnt offering and its offerings, as mentioned in (Ex 29:38-42, Num 28:1-8).

23.17.3.en: b- The offerings of the beginning of the month, which are mentioned in (Num 28:11-15) and include:

23.17.5.en: Two young bullocks with their offerings, three tenths of flour mingled with oil and half a hin of wine for each bullock.

23.17.6.en: A ram with its offering, two tenths of flour mingled with oil, with a third of a hin of wine poured on it.

23.17.7.en: Seven lambs of the first year with their offerings, one tenth of flour mingled with oil, and their drink offering is a fourth part of a hin of wine for each lamb.

23.17.8.en: 2- A sin offering, which is a kid.

23.17.9.en: c- After the morning burnt offering and the offerings of the beginning of the month are offered, the trumpets are blown, and then the offerings of the Feast of Trumpets mentioned in (Num 29:1-6) are offered, which are:

23.17.11.en: A bullock and its offering, which is three tenths of flour mingled with oil, with its drink offering, which is half a hin of wine.

23.17.12.en: A ram and its offering, two tenths of flour mingled with oil, and its drink offering, a third of a hin of wine.

23.17.13.en: Seven lambs of the first year and their offering, which is one tenth of flour mingled with oil, and their drink offering, a fourth part of a hin of wine.

23.17.14.en: Then the priest blesses the people with the words of blessing mentioned in (Num 6:24-26), and the people are bowing down, and then they depart to their homes. After the building of the Temple of Solomon, they used to go to the synagogues to hear readings from the Holy Scriptures and then return to their houses.

23.17.15.en: d- The people return in the evening to attend the offering of the evening burnt offering.

23.17.16.en: When God reminds you to return to Him and live with Him, do not neglect His voice, whether His speech is from the Holy Bible, or through one of the loved ones around you, or in any other form, for these are divine messages or trumpets that declare God's love and His longing for you.

23.18.0.en: This feast is also called the Feast of Forgiveness or of seeking forgiveness, and its date was the tenth of the seventh month of the religious year, which is the month of Tishrin the First, corresponding to the month of October today. It was a holy convocation on which the people refrained from their material work and gave themselves wholly to worship. They fasted on this day and humbled themselves with repentance and contrition before God. This feast signifies the redemption of Christ and His atonement for the sins of humanity, and corresponds to it in the New Testament Good Friday. At this feast they offer the offerings mentioned in detail in (ch. 16), which are:

23.18.1.en: a- The burnt offerings of the permanent morning and evening service.

23.18.2.en: b- The sacrifices of the feast, which are:

23.18.3.en: 1- A bullock as a sin offering for the priests.

23.18.4.en: 2- A goat as a sin offering for the people, in addition to the goat of Azazel, which is let go in the wilderness.

23.18.5.en: And also additional sacrifices, which are:

23.18.6.en: 3- A burnt offering, which is a ram offered for the priests.

23.18.7.en: 4- A bullock as a burnt offering for the people, with its offerings and drink offerings.

23.18.8.en: 5- Seven lambs of the first year as a burnt offering for the people, with their offerings and drink offerings.

23.18.9.en: 6- A sin offering, which is a goat.

23.18.10.en: All these sacrifices and their offerings were already explained in detail in (ch. 16).

23.19.0.en: Whoever refuses to humble himself, that is, to fast on this day, this means his lack of repentance and his need of God's forgiveness, so the Law commands that he be put to death for his refusal to believe in God and repent of his sins.

23.20.0.en: Likewise whoever makes light of this great feast and is occupied with his material work shows his lack of concern for repentance and God's forgiveness, so God declares that He will destroy him, that is, he dies by being put to death or dies in any form.

23.21.0.en: Therefore God commands abstaining from all material work at this feast, and this is to be applied throughout their lives and in the generations after them, until Christ comes and offers redemption and atonement for humanity on the Cross.

23.22.0.en: Ye shall celebrate your sabbath: you shall rest from your works.

23.22.1.en: God sets the time of freedom from work at this feast, which is the whole day, beginning from its eve, that is, the evening of the ninth day of the month, and then throughout the daytime of the tenth day.

23.22.2.en: Take care of your daily repentance before God so that you receive His forgiveness, renew your vigor and begin with new hope to make up for what you have missed, and set out on a positive spiritual life in His worship and service.

23.23.0.en: The Feast of Tabernacles is one of the important feasts among the Jews, and its date is the fifteenth of the seventh month of the religious year, which is the month of Tishrin the First, that is, Ethanim, corresponding to the month of October. It is kept for seven days in addition to the eighth day, which is a holy convocation; that is, the feast is kept eight days and the eighth day is an official holiday.

23.23.1.en: It is like the Feast of the Passover in its importance, since the Passover and Unleavened Bread are also kept eight days. Because of the importance of this feast it is mentioned several times in the Holy Bible: it is mentioned in the days of Solomon (2 Chr 8:13), in the days of Nehemiah (Neh 8:13-18) and in the days of Christ (Jn 7:2). This feast is also called the Feast of Ingathering, since on it all the summer crops and fruits such as grapes and olives are gathered; it is the third of the agricultural feasts after the Feasts of Firstfruits and Pentecost.

23.23.2.en: The spiritual meanings of this feast are:

23.23.3.en: 1- Thanking God for His kindnesses after gathering all the crops of the year.

23.23.4.en: 2- Remembering the days of their sojourn in the wilderness of Sinai when they lived in tents or movable booths; so that they would not forget God's kindnesses to them in bringing them to the Promised Land, they kept this feast.

23.23.5.en: 3- This feast gives the meaning of the sojourn in the world and attachment to heavenly things, and this is a meaning that continues in the New Testament, as Zechariah prophesied (Zech 14:16) ....

23.23.6.en: This feast is the last of the feasts in the religious year and one of the three most important feasts, at which all the males of the people of God, on behalf of their families, must gather and stand before the house of God. These feasts are the Passover, Pentecost and then the Feast of Tabernacles.

23.23.7.en: They used to make these booths from the branches of trees (v. 42), and they have different forms as shown in the attached picture.

23.24.0.en: This feast is kept eight days. On the first and the eighth they free themselves for worship and do no material work, and on the six days between them their celebration of the feast and their dwelling in the booths continue. At this feast, on the first day, they gather the branches of trees and set up a shelter over the bronze altar, and bring water from the Pool of Siloam and pour it on the bronze altar over the morning burnt offering together with wine, so that they may remember not only their sojourn in the wilderness of Sinai but also their being given water to drink from the rock, which signifies Christ (1 Cor 10:4). The water signifies the work of the Holy Spirit, who was poured out on the believers in the Church of the New Testament.

23.25.0.en: The fire offering of the Lord that is offered in the seven days is mentioned for us in the Book of Numbers in (Num 29:12-39), and it is: a- Burnt offerings:

23.25.1.en: 1- Thirteen bullocks on the first day, decreasing by one bullock each day until the seventh day, when there are seven bullocks, and their total is seventy bullocks. And with each bullock, three tenths of flour mingled with oil.

23.25.2.en: 2- Two rams each day, with two tenths of flour mingled with oil for each ram.

23.25.3.en: 3- Fourteen lambs of the first year each day, with one tenth of flour mingled with oil for each lamb.

23.25.4.en: b- A sin offering: consisting of a kid of the goats.

23.25.5.en: c- The daily morning and evening burnt offering.

23.25.6.en: d- Peace offerings, vows and freewill offerings, which are the voluntary offerings from the people.

23.25.7.en: As for the eighth day of the Feast of Tabernacles, it is a solemn assembly, that is, giving oneself wholly to worship and leaving the daily work as happened on the first day, because if the Feast of Tabernacles signifies the sojourn in the world, then the sojourn must be joined with being occupied with the love of God and His worship, which is the purpose of life.

23.25.8.en: And the fire offerings of the Lord on this day, as the Book of Numbers mentions them for us (Num 29:35-39), are:

23.25.10.en: 1- A bullock with its offering, which is three tenths of flour mingled with oil.

23.25.11.en: 2- One ram with its offering, two tenths of flour mingled with oil.

23.25.12.en: 3- Seven lambs of the first year with their offerings, which are one tenth of flour mingled with oil for each lamb.

23.25.13.en: b- A sin offering, which is a kid of the goats.

23.25.14.en: c- The permanent burnt offering, morning and evening, with their offerings.

23.25.15.en: d- Peace offerings, vows and freewill offerings, which are the voluntary offerings that the people offer to God.

23.26.0.en: He closes with this verse, declaring that the above are the seven feasts of the Lord, which He calls seasons and holy convocations to God, with the sacrifices and offerings offered on each day of these feasts, as a showing of man's love and thanks to God.

23.27.0.en: In addition to the sacrifices offered at the feasts, the sacrifices offered on the days of the Sabbaths are also offered, on which the morning and evening burnt offering is double that of ordinary days. Likewise the voluntary offerings that the people offer to God are also added.

23.28.0.en: Here he stresses the importance of celebrating the Feast of Tabernacles, which they keep for eight days. The first day is a time of freedom for worship and a holiday from material work, after gathering the last harvest of the summer crops, and the eighth day is also a holiday.

23.28.1.en: The first day is the fifteenth of the seventh month and the eighth day is the twenty-second of it, so the feast extends eight days, but freedom for worship is only on the first and last day.

23.29.1.en: Willows: a plant that grows by watercourses.

23.29.2.en: He shows what happens at this feast, that is, the Feast of Tabernacles: the people gather palm branches and large tree branches and make booths from them, and complete them with small palm fronds and small tree branches, and decorate them with the cheerful fruit of trees, and they go to the Pool of Siloam to draw water and pour it on the bronze altar with wine, and they rejoice and go around the altar seven times, in remembrance of going around Jericho, so that they remember the Lord's victories with them and rejoice.

23.30.0.en: God stresses to them the celebration of this great feast for seven days throughout their days, as long as the Levitical priesthood stands.

23.31.0.en: All the Jews dwell in these booths that they make in the outer court of the house of God, in the streets of Jerusalem and on the mountains, and no one dwells in his house, so that they remember their sojourn from the world and their attachment to heaven.

23.32.0.en: He also reminds them of their dwelling in booths, the tents in which they lived forty years in the wilderness of Sinai, and of God's care for them with manna and quail and water from the rock and His protection of them from their enemies.

23.33.0.en: Moses told the people of God all that the Lord had commanded them concerning the feasts, so that they might carry it out and enjoy the worship of God and fellowship with Him.

23.33.1.en: Always remember, when you enjoy the material things of life, that God is the one who gives them to you, and thank Him; and on the other hand, discipline yourself in the use of material things so that your feelings of love toward God may be set free and nothing may hinder you from Him.
